terms.sub: Alveolar Gas Equation and Partial Pressures
clues: It incorporates inspired oxygen tension, arterial PCO2, and the respiratory exchange ratio (R = 0.8)
It allows clinicians to calculate the alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient from an arterial blood gas
This formula calculates mean alveolar oxygen partial pressure as PAO2 = PiO2 - (PaCO2 / R)
It explains why CO2 transfers ~20 times faster than O2 due to its 24-fold higher aqueous solubility
Pulmonary fibrosis impairs gas transfer under this law by increasing membrane thickness (T)
It states that gas transfer across a tissue sheet is proportional to surface area and partial pressure difference, and inversely proportional to thickness
It is measured clinically using a single breath of trace carbon monoxide (DLCO)
It decreases in both emphysema (loss of surface area) and pulmonary fibrosis (increased barrier thickness)
It quantifies the volume of gas transferred across the alveolar-capillary membrane per minute per mmHg of partial pressure gradient
It is absent in monomeric myoglobin, which therefore has a hyperbolic dissociation curve
Binding of the first oxygen molecule breaks salt bridges and transitions hemoglobin from the T state to the R state
This subunit interaction gives the adult oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve its characteristic sigmoidal shape

terms.sub: Carbon Dioxide Transport and Chloride Shift
clues: Also called the Hamburger phenomenon, it makes venous hematocrit slightly higher than arterial hematocrit
It is mediated by the red blood cell Band 3 (AE1) anion exchanger
Bicarbonate generated inside systemic capillary erythrocytes exits into plasma in exchange for Cl- influx to maintain electroneutrality

terms.sub: Carbon Dioxide Transport and Chloride Shift
clues: It is the reciprocal counterpart to the Bohr effect
Deoxygenated hemoglobin buffers H+ ions better and forms carbamino compounds more readily than oxyhemoglobin
It describes how oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs promotes unloading of carbon dioxide

terms.sub: Carbon Dioxide Transport and Chloride Shift
clues: It accounts for approximately 20 to 23 percent of total CO2 transport in venous blood
It forms without the need for carbonic anhydrase and does not bind the heme iron atom
It is the compound formed when carbon dioxide binds reversibly to terminal amino groups of globin chains
Hypoxemia from this mechanism fails to correct fully even when breathing 100% oxygen
Bronchial veins and cardiac Thebesian veins create a small physiological version of this (~1-2% of cardiac output)
It occurs when deoxygenated mixed-venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli (VA/Q = 0) and enters the systemic arterial circulation
